claim: Sst-Cre and Pvalb-Cre mouse strains express Cre-recombinase under control of the Sst or Pvalb promoter.
source: To target our opsins to either Sst+ or Pvalb+ cells, we used Sst-Cre and Pvalb-Cre knock-in lines (JAX strains 013044/RRID:IMSR_JAX:013044 and 008069/RRID:IMSR_JAX:008069, with mixed C57BL/6;129S4 and C57BL/6;129P2 backgrounds, respectively).
evidence: Cited from established mouse strain information with specific JAX strain numbers

claim: Sst-Cre and Pvalb-Cre strains drive expression of Cre in Sst+ and Pvalb+ interneurons of the cortex and hippocampus with minimal (<10%) leak.
source: These strains drive expression of Cre in Sst+ and Pvalb+ interneurons of the cortex and hippocampus with minimal (<10%) leak (Taniguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Taniguchi et al., 2011

claim: In Arch/Sst mice, the specificity of GFP labeling for Sst+ neurons was 89 ± 4%.
source: In Arch/Sst mice, the percentage of GFP labeled neurons that showed Sst fluorescence (i.e., specificity) was 89 ± 4%
evidence: Measured from immunostaining data in the study

claim: In Arch/Sst mice, the efficiency of GFP labeling for Sst+ neurons was 91 ± 2%.
source: and the percentage of Sst labeled neurons that were GFP-labeled (i.e., efficiency) was 91 ± 2%
evidence: Measured from immunostaining data in the study

claim: In Arch/Pvalb mice, the specificity of GFP labeling for Pvalb+ neurons was 93 ± 2%.
source: and in Arch/Pvalb mice the specificity was 93 ± 2%
evidence: Measured from immunostaining data in the study

claim: In Arch/Pvalb mice, the efficiency of GFP labeling for Pvalb+ neurons was 89 ± 7%.
source: and the efficiency was 89 ± 7%, consistent with previous reports (Adesnik et al., 2012; Cardin et al., 2009; Kerlin et al., 2010; Kvitsiani et al., 2013; Pfeffer et al., 2013; Sohal et al., 2009; Taniguchi et al., 2011)
evidence: Measured from immunostaining data in the study and consistent with cited literature

claim: Of the frequency-tuned units in Arch/Sst mice, 44 of 70 units had sound-evoked firing rates that were significantly increased by light.
source: Of the units with frequency-tuned responses (see Materials and methods; Arch/Sst: n = 70 of 96 units; Arch/Pvalb: n = 59 of 76 units), the majority had sound-evoked FRs that were significantly increased by light (Arch/Sst: n = 44 of 70 units; Arch/Pvalb: n = 41 of 59 units)
evidence: Directly measured from electrophysiological recordings

claim: Of the frequency-tuned units in Arch/Pvalb mice, 41 of 59 units had sound-evoked firing rates that were significantly increased by light.
source: Of the units with frequency-tuned responses (see Materials and methods; Arch/Sst: n = 70 of 96 units; Arch/Pvalb: n = 59 of 76 units), the majority had sound-evoked FRs that were significantly increased by light (Arch/Sst: n = 44 of 70 units; Arch/Pvalb: n = 41 of 59 units)
evidence: Directly measured from electrophysiological recordings

claim: In Arch/Sst mice, 11 of 70 frequency-tuned units had responses that were significantly suppressed by light.
source: a minority had responses that were significantly suppressed by light (Arch/Sst: n = 11 of 70 units; Arch/Pvalb: n = 5 of 59 units)
evidence: Directly measured from electrophysiological recordings

claim: In Arch/Pvalb mice, 5 of 59 frequency-tuned units had responses that were significantly suppressed by light.
source: a minority had responses that were significantly suppressed by light (Arch/Sst: n = 11 of 70 units; Arch/Pvalb: n = 5 of 59 units)
evidence: Directly measured from electrophysiological recordings

claim: The proportions of linear transformation types produced by inactivation of Sst+ cells were significantly different from those produced by inactivation of Pvalb+ cells (Fisher's exact test p=0.0015).
source: However, the proportions of linear transformation types produced by inactivation of Sst+ cells were significantly different from those produced by inactivation of Pvalb+ cells (Fisher's exact test p=0.0015; Figure 3b).
evidence: Statistical test performed on experimental data

claim: Inactivating Sst+ cells had a significantly larger effect on the response gain than inactivating Pvalb+ cells (rank-sum p=0.01).
source: To quantitatively compare the effects of inactivating Sst+ or Pvalb+ cells on response gain (i.e., the magnitude of the multiplicative component), we compared the distributions of the slope values obtained from the linear regression analyses (Figure 3c) and found that inactivating Sst+ cells had a significantly larger effect on the response gain than inactivating Pvalb+ cells (rank-sum p=0.01).
evidence: Statistical comparison of slope coefficients from linear regression analysis

claim: Inactivating Pvalb+ cells had a significantly larger effect on the magnitude of the additive component compared to inactivating Sst+ cells (rank-sum p=1.5 × 10−4).
source: Furthermore, inactivating Pvalb+ cells had a significantly larger effect on the magnitude of the additive component compared to inactivating Sst+ cells (rank-sum p=1.5 × 10−4; Figure 3d).
evidence: Statistical comparison of y-intercepts from linear regression analysis

claim: The differences between the effects of inactivating Sst+ versus Pvalb+ cells were more prominent among broad-spiking units than narrow-spiking units.
source: These differences between the effects of inactivating Sst+ versus Pvalb+ cells were more prominent among broad-spiking units than narrow-spiking units (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Comparison of effects across different unit types shown in supplementary figure

claim: The larger additive effect produced by inactivating Pvalb+ cells was not entirely due to increases in spontaneous activity.
source: Interestingly, this larger additive effect produced by inactivating Pvalb+ cells was not entirely due to increases in spontaneous activity, as performing linear regression on baseline-subtracted responses (defined as sound-evoked FR minus spontaneous FR; Figure 3—figure supplement 3a,b) revealed similar differences in both the slopes and y-intercepts (Figure 3—figure supplement 3c,d)
evidence: Analysis of baseline-subtracted responses shown in supplementary figures

claim: The additive effect produced by inactivation of Pvalb+ cells includes a substantial contribution from sound-evoked responses that are not frequency selective.
source: implying that the additive effect produced by inactivation of Pvalb+ cells must include a substantial contribution from sound-evoked responses that are not frequency selective.
evidence: Inference from baseline-subtracted analysis showing persistent additive effects

claim: In ChR2/Sst mice, 64 of 97 frequency-tuned units had responses to tones that were significantly reduced by light.
source: Of the frequency-tuned units (ChR2/Sst: n = 97 of 163 units; ChR2/Pvalb: n = 103 of 160 units; see Materials and methods), the majority had responses to tones that were significantly reduced by light (ChR2/Sst: n = 64 of 97 units; ChR2/Pvalb: n = 62 of 103 units)
evidence: Directly measured from electrophysiological recordings

claim: In ChR2/Pvalb mice, 62 of 103 frequency-tuned units had responses to tones that were significantly reduced by light.
source: Of the frequency-tuned units (ChR2/Sst: n = 97 of 163 units; ChR2/Pvalb: n = 103 of 160 units; see Materials and methods), the majority had responses to tones that were significantly reduced by light (ChR2/Sst: n = 64 of 97 units; ChR2/Pvalb: n = 62 of 103 units)
evidence: Directly measured from electrophysiological recordings

claim: The proportions of significant linear transformations observed when activating Sst+ cells and activating Pvalb+ cells were similar to one another (Fisher's exact test p=0.51).
source: Counterintuitively, given the observation that inactivation of Sst+ versus Pvalb+ interneurons caused different effects on the gain and tuning of tone responses, the proportions of significant linear transformations observed when activating Sst+ cells and activating Pvalb+ cells were similar to one another (Fisher's exact test p=0.51; Figure 5b).
evidence: Statistical test performed on experimental data

claim: The distributions of the slope values obtained from the linear regression analyses were similar for activation of Sst+ and Pvalb+ cells (slopes: rank-sum p=0.68).
source: Furthermore, the distributions of the slope values and the distributions of the y-intercept values obtained from the linear regression analyses were similar (slopes: rank-sum p=0.68; Figure 5c; y-intercepts: rank-sum p=0.77; Figure 5d)
evidence: Statistical comparison of slope coefficients from linear regression analysis

claim: The distributions of the y-intercept values obtained from the linear regression analyses were similar for activation of Sst+ and Pvalb+ cells (y-intercepts: rank-sum p=0.77).
source: Furthermore, the distributions of the slope values and the distributions of the y-intercept values obtained from the linear regression analyses were similar (slopes: rank-sum p=0.68; Figure 5c; y-intercepts: rank-sum p=0.77; Figure 5d)
evidence: Statistical comparison of y-intercepts from linear regression analysis

claim: Optogenetic activation of putative Sst+ and Pvalb+ interneurons had a larger effect on spontaneous firing rates than sound-evoked firing rates.
source: Interestingly, optogenetic activation of putative Sst+ and Pvalb+ interneurons had a larger effect on spontaneous FRs (putative Sst+: FR ratio = 3.9 ± 2.9; putative Pvalb+: FR ratio = 2.5 ± 0.8), than sound-evoked FRs (putative Sst+: FR ratio = 2.9 ± 1.5; putative Pvalb+: FR ratio = 1.5 ± 0.2).
evidence: Comparison of firing rate ratios from putative interneuron recordings

claim: Putative interneurons that were not generally active without light often showed firing rates well above 30 Hz during the light.
source: Moreover, even putative interneurons that were not generally active without light (sound-evoked rate of less than 5 Hz; putative Sst+: n = 7 units; putative Pvalb+: n = 1 unit) often showed FRs well above 30 Hz during the light (putative Sst+: evoked rate = 35.04 ± 28.3 Hz; putative Pvalb+: evoked rate = 54.5 Hz).
evidence: Measured firing rates from putative interneurons during optogenetic activation

claim: Activation increases the number of stimulus-independent spikes generated by both interneuron populations, potentially masking normal stimulus-driven function.
source: Together, these results suggest that activation increases the number of stimulus-independent spikes generated by both interneuron populations, potentially masking normal stimulus-driven function.
evidence: Inference from the observation that activation affects spontaneous rates more than evoked rates

claim: Inactivating Sst+ cells significantly increased information-per-trial (sign-rank p=0.022).
source: The effects of inactivating Sst+ cells on information-per-trial were significantly different from the effects of inactivating Pvalb+ cells (rank-sum p=7.1 × 10−6; Figure 6b,c): inactivating Sst+ cells significantly increased information-per-trial (sign-rank p=0.022)
evidence: Statistical test on mutual information calculations

claim: Inactivating Pvalb+ cells significantly decreased information-per-trial (sign-rank p=1.3 × 10−4).
source: while inactivating Pvalb+ cells significantly decreased it (sign-rank p=1.3 × 10−4).
evidence: Statistical test on mutual information calculations

claim: The effects of inactivating Sst+ cells on information-per-trial were significantly different from the effects of inactivating Pvalb+ cells (rank-sum p=7.1 × 10−6).
source: The effects of inactivating Sst+ cells on information-per-trial were significantly different from the effects of inactivating Pvalb+ cells (rank-sum p=7.1 × 10−6; Figure 6b,c)
evidence: Statistical comparison of information-per-trial changes between groups

claim: The effects on information-per-spike of inactivating Sst+ cells versus Pvalb+ cells were significantly different (rank-sum p=1.2 × 10−5).
source: The effects on information-per-spike of inactivating Sst+ cells versus Pvalb+ cells were significantly different (rank-sum p=1.2 × 10−5), inconsistent with the notion that the observed differences in information transfer were due to differences in firing rate modulation (Figure 6d,e).
evidence: Statistical comparison of information-per-spike changes between groups

claim: The observed differences in information transfer were not due to differences in firing rate modulation.
source: The effects on information-per-spike of inactivating Sst+ cells versus Pvalb+ cells were significantly different (rank-sum p=1.2 × 10−5), inconsistent with the notion that the observed differences in information transfer were due to differences in firing rate modulation (Figure 6d,e).
evidence: Inference from the finding that information-per-spike differences persist after normalizing for firing rate

claim: Neither activation of Sst+ cells nor activation of Pvalb+ cells significantly changed information-per-trial (ChR2/Sst: sign-rank p=0.53; ChR2/Pvalb: sign-rank p=0.63).
source: In contrast, activating Sst+ cells and activating Pvalb+ cells did not differentially impact information-per-trial (rank-sum p=0.85): indeed, neither activation of Sst+ cells nor activation of Pvalb+ cells significantly changed information-per-trial (ChR2/Sst: sign-rank p=0.53; ChR2/Pvalb: sign-rank p=0.63; Figure 6g,h).
evidence: Statistical tests on mutual information calculations

claim: Activating Sst+ cells and activating Pvalb+ cells did not differentially impact information-per-trial (rank-sum p=0.85).
source: In contrast, activating Sst+ cells and activating Pvalb+ cells did not differentially impact information-per-trial (rank-sum p=0.85)
evidence: Statistical comparison of information-per-trial changes between groups

claim: Multiplicatively modulating the firing of the upstream layer produces multiplication of the downstream neuron's net drive.
source: Multiplicatively modulating the firing of the upstream layer (Figure 7b) linearly increases the firing rate of each of the weighted inputs (Figure 7c), which sum in the downstream neuron to produce multiplication of its net drive (Figure 7d).
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling shown in Figure 7

claim: Additively modulating a single input produces a constant (additive) increase in the downstream neuron's net drive across all stimulus frequencies.
source: Similarly, additively modulating a single input (Figure 7e) produces a constant increase in the firing rate of each weighted input (Figure 7f), which, summed in the downstream neuron, leads to a constant (additive) increase in its net drive across all stimulus frequencies (Figure 7g).
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling shown in Figure 7

claim: Inactivation of interneurons preserves the single-cell effects of multiplication and addition at the network level in this simple model.
source: Thus, inactivation of interneurons preserves the single-cell effects of multiplication and addition at the network level in this simple model.
evidence: Conclusion from the modeling results

claim: Subtractive suppression does not linearly suppress the firing of the input neurons because the weakest responses are suppressed below the nonlinear spiking threshold, creating a 'floor effect' at the edges of the tuning curve.
source: In contrast, subtractive suppression does not linearly suppress the firing of the input neurons because the weakest responses are suppressed below the nonlinear spiking threshold, creating a 'floor effect' at the edges of the tuning curve.
evidence: Explanation of model behavior based on threshold nonlinearity

claim: Subtractive suppression appears division-like from the perspective of the downstream neuron.
source: In the downstream neuron, these nonlinear floor effects at the edges sum to produce the strongest suppression at the center of the tuning curve (Figure 7n), and thus, downstream, appear division-like (Figure 7k,n).
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling shown in Figure 7

claim: Aspects of the network state such as its baseline firing rate determine the regime wherein asymmetric effects between activation and inactivation will be observed.
source: Importantly, aspects of the network state such as its baseline firing rate determine the regime wherein such asymmetric effects between activation and inactivation will be observed (Figure 8).
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling shown in Figure 8

claim: In a network with high spontaneous activity, the range of interneuron manipulation levels over which the neural circuit behaves linearly is relatively large.
source: For example, in a network with high spontaneous activity (Figure 8j), interneurons must be activated more strongly in order to suppress their targets' firing rates below the spiking threshold; thus the range of interneuron manipulation levels over which the neural circuit behaves linearly is relatively large (Figure 8l).
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling shown in Figure 8

claim: In a network with low spontaneous activity, the linear operating range of the network becomes relatively small.
source: On the other hand, in a network with low spontaneous activity, in which the edges of the tuning curves already lie below threshold (Figure 8p), even small additive increases in firing rates are impacted by threshold nonlinearities; thus the linear operating range of the network becomes relatively small (Figure 8r).
evidence: Demonstrated through computational modeling shown in Figure 8

claim: The qualitative conclusions drawn from optogenetic manipulations are sensitive to both the details of the manipulation and the state of the circuit in which the manipulation is performed.
source: These results highlight that the qualitative conclusions drawn from optogenetic manipulations are sensitive to both the details of the manipulation and the state of the circuit in which the manipulation is performed.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from modeling results

claim: Inhibition shapes the gain and tuning of sensory responses throughout the neocortex.
source: Throughout the neocortex, inhibition shapes the gain and tuning of sensory responses (Kyriazi et al., 1996; Tsumoto and Sato, 1985; Wang et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: Inhibition controls the precise timing of evoked action potentials.
source: controls the precise timing of evoked action potentials (Akiyama et al., 2004; Gabernet et al., 2005; Hasenstaub et al., 2005; Poo and Isaacson, 2009; Wehr and Zador, 2003)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: Inhibition can coordinate rhythmic activity, which gates sensory responses and modulates information processing.
source: and can coordinate rhythmic activity, which gates sensory responses and modulates information processing (Cardin et al., 2009; Deans et al., 2001; Hasenstaub et al., 2005; Sohal et al., 2009).

claim: GABAergic interneurons comprise a minority of cells in the cortex.
source: Although they comprise a minority of cells in the cortex, the GABAergic interneurons that provide this inhibition are strikingly diverse (rev. [Petilla Interneuron Nomenclature et al., 2008])
evidence: Established knowledge cited from review

claim: GABAergic interneurons are strikingly diverse.
source: Although they comprise a minority of cells in the cortex, the GABAergic interneurons that provide this inhibition are strikingly diverse (rev. [Petilla Interneuron Nomenclature et al., 2008])

claim: Unique combinations of gene expression, electrophysiological properties, morphology, and connectivity define multiple interneuron types.
source: unique combinations of gene expression, electrophysiological properties, morphology, and connectivity define multiple interneuron types, and likely allow each interneuron type to exert a unique mode of control over cortical function.

claim: Each interneuron type likely exerts a unique mode of control over cortical function.
source: unique combinations of gene expression, electrophysiological properties, morphology, and connectivity define multiple interneuron types, and likely allow each interneuron type to exert a unique mode of control over cortical function.

claim: Optogenetics enables reversible and selective activation or inactivation of interneuron firing in vivo.
source: Recent advances in molecular techniques, such as optogenetics (Boyden et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2011), chemogenetics (Armbruster et al., 2007), and more recently magnetogenetics (Wheeler et al., 2016), have transcended traditional methods of probing cell function, enabling reversible and selective activation or inactivation of interneuron firing in vivo.
evidence: Established knowledge about optogenetic techniques with citations

claim: An implicit assumption underlying much optogenetic work is that one can directly read out a cell type's function by tonically modulating its firing down or up.
source: An implicit assumption underlying much of this work is that one can directly read out a cell type's function, and infer its specialized operations, by tonically modulating its firing down or up
evidence: Identification of an assumption in the field

claim: The response features or computations weakened by inactivating a cell population are assumed to be specifically those that the cell population normally supports.
source: in other words, that the response features or computations weakened by inactivating a cell population are specifically those that the cell population normally supports, that these features will be strengthened when the same population is activated, and that the natural differences in cortical function between cell populations may be read out, and interpreted, using these same strategies.
evidence: Identification of an assumption in the field

claim: Inactivation of Sst+ interneurons increased response gain.
source: We found that inactivation of Sst+ interneurons increased response gain, while inactivation of Pvalb+ interneurons weakened tuning and decreased information transfer, implying that these two neuron types support specific, separable functions in the auditory cortex.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Inactivation of Pvalb+ interneurons weakened tuning and decreased information transfer.
source: We found that inactivation of Sst+ interneurons increased response gain, while inactivation of Pvalb+ interneurons weakened tuning and decreased information transfer, implying that these two neuron types support specific, separable functions in the auditory cortex.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Sst+ and Pvalb+ interneurons support specific, separable functions in the auditory cortex.
source: We found that inactivation of Sst+ interneurons increased response gain, while inactivation of Pvalb+ interneurons weakened tuning and decreased information transfer, implying that these two neuron types support specific, separable functions in the auditory cortex.
evidence: Inference from inactivation experiments

claim: Activating Sst+ and Pvalb+ interneurons revealed no differences in their effects on gain, tuning, or information transfer.
source: Yet activating Sst+ and Pvalb+ interneurons revealed no such differences.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Relatively small changes in key parameters such as spontaneous activity or strength of the light manipulation determine whether activation and inactivation produce consistent or paradoxical conclusions regarding interneurons' computational functions.
source: We used a simple network model to understand this asymmetry, and showed how relatively small changes in key parameters, such as spontaneous activity or strength of the light manipulation, determined whether activation and inactivation would produce consistent or paradoxical conclusions regarding interneurons' computational functions.
evidence: Conclusion from modeling results

claim: Activation of interneurons may be particularly likely to mask normal interneuron function because it targets interneurons that are not normally active during a stimulus response.
source: We propose that activation may be particularly likely to mask normal interneuron function because it targets interneurons that are not normally active during a stimulus response, and it is likely to obscure distinctions between linear transformations within a nonlinear network
evidence: Proposed explanation based on experimental and modeling results

claim: Activation is likely to obscure distinctions between linear transformations within a nonlinear network.
source: We propose that activation may be particularly likely to mask normal interneuron function because it targets interneurons that are not normally active during a stimulus response, and it is likely to obscure distinctions between linear transformations within a nonlinear network

claim: Inactivation targets only the normally active subset of interneurons.

claim: Inactivation is more likely to preserve distinctions between linear transformation types within a nonlinear network.

claim: Bidirectional manipulations – activation and inactivation – are widely used to identify the functions supported by specific cortical interneuron types.
source: Bidirectional manipulations – activation and inactivation – are widely used to identify the functions supported by specific cortical interneuron types.

source: This implies that seemingly minor experimental details can qualitatively change the readout of a neural population's role in computation, and that the conclusions we draw regarding neuronal function can be influenced, even distorted, by the precise way in which the neuronal populations are manipulated.
